## Example 7.2 {#ss7-example-7-2 .lim-lesson .lim-derivation}

Consider the formula for the $n$th partial sum of a geometric series:

$$S_n=\frac{a(1-\textcolor{#b55224}{r^n})}{1-r}.$$

**(a)** Under what condition do you suspect that the sum of a geometric series approaches a finite number? That is, the series has a ‘limiting sum’.

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="0"}

$$|r|<1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\textcolor{#b55224}{r^n\longrightarrow0}$$

:::

**(b)** Find the value of the limiting sum.

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

$$S_n\longrightarrow\frac{a(1-\textcolor{#b55224}{0})}{1-r}=\frac{a}{1-r}$$

:::

<p class="booklet-cue">Booklet p. 44 · Example 7.2</p>

::: notes

The finite-sum formula requires r≠1. For a non-zero first term, a finite limiting sum exists exactly when |r|<1. Click 1 identifies r^n→0, including negative r between −1 and 0. Click 2 substitutes this limit. If |r|≥1 the terms do not approach zero, so the partial sums cannot converge. This avoids extending the quotient outside its convergence domain. If a=0 the recurrence is the all-zero sequence and its sum is 0 regardless of the chosen multiplier.

:::
